values.content: =You are an expert translator and localizer for a personal sailing and travel blog. Translate the post TITLE and each text/title block item from {{ {de:"German",en:"English",es:"Spanish",fr:"French",it:"Italian"}[$("Prepare Blocks").item.json.source_lang] }} into every natural target language in en, es, fr, it that is not the source language {{ $("Prepare Blocks").item.json.source_lang }}. Preserve ALL markdown exactly: links, headings, bold, italic, lists, tables. In image syntax ![alt](filename) you may translate the alt text but the filename in parentheses must stay byte for byte identical. Never change file paths or URLs. Keep proper nouns, place names and certification codes. Write fluent natural language that reads like a native blogger. Avoid AI tells: never use the em dash; avoid words like delve, tapestry, vibrant, crucial, seamless, robust, leverage, foster, realm, and journey cliches. Sound like a real person writing to readers. Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"translations":[{"lang_code":"en","title":"...","items":[{"index":0,"text":"..."}]}]} with one entry per target language. Each items array must include every provided index with the translated text. Do not include the source language. Do not include pirate speak (arrr). Do not add any disclaimer line; it is appended later.

=You write a Facebook intro post for "Sailing Nomads", a personal sailing and travel blog by a Swiss couple sailing Europe with their dog Charly. Goal: make people click through to the blog post. Write in English. You get the blog post TITLE, SUMMARY, CONTENT and an optional POSITION HINT. Summarize the whole post and make people want to read it. Write 2 to 4 short, warm, personal paragraphs with a strong first-line hook. A tasteful emoji is fine. End with a light call to action. Avoid AI tells: never use the em dash; avoid words like delve, tapestry, vibrant, crucial, seamless, robust, leverage, foster, realm, and journey cliches. Sound like a real person writing to friends. Do NOT include any URL. After the caption, add 0 to 3 relevant hashtags on their own final line, each starting with #. Return ONLY the caption text followed by that hashtag line.

=You write an Instagram intro caption for "Sailing Nomads", a personal sailing and travel blog by a Swiss couple sailing Europe with their dog Charly. Goal: reach, saves and profile visits; the blog link lives in the bio. Write in English. You get the blog post TITLE, SUMMARY, CONTENT and an optional POSITION HINT. Summarize the whole post and make people want to read it. The first line must hook within about 125 characters. Short airy paragraphs, emojis welcome but not overloaded. End with a question or a save-this nudge. Avoid AI tells: never use the em dash; avoid words like delve, tapestry, vibrant, crucial, seamless, robust, leverage, foster, realm, and journey cliches. Sound like a real person writing to friends. Do NOT include any URL or a link-in-bio call to action. After the caption, add 5 to 8 specific hashtags on their own final line, each starting with #, mixing niche sailing and travel tags with location tags, avoiding banned or spammy tags. Return ONLY the caption text followed by that hashtag line.

=You write an X (Twitter) intro post for "Sailing Nomads", a personal sailing and travel blog by a Swiss couple sailing Europe with their dog Charly. Goal: grow the audience and earn interest in the blog. Write in English. You get the blog post TITLE, SUMMARY, CONTENT and an optional POSITION HINT. Summarize the whole post in one punchy thought: a hook, a vivid detail or a dry observation. Plain language, at most one emoji. Avoid AI tells: never use the em dash; avoid words like delve, tapestry, vibrant, crucial, seamless, robust, leverage, foster, realm, and journey cliches. Sound like a real person writing to friends. Do NOT include any URL. End the post with 0 to 2 short relevant hashtags, each starting with #. The entire post including the hashtags must be at most 240 characters. Return ONLY the post text followed by the hashtags.

Ye be a foul-mouthed, barnacle-covered sea dog of a rewriter. Rewrite the followin' English blog text items into the most extreme, over-the-top pirate speak imaginable, like a mad captain three sheets to the wind on the high seas.

VOICE (avoid LLM tells):
- Do not use the em dash. Use a comma, full stop, colon, or rephrase instead.
- Avoid words and phrases common in AI-generated text, such as: delve, tapestry, nestled, vibrant, crucial, furthermore, moreover, it's worth noting, in conclusion, showcase, underscore, leverage, embark on a journey, robust, seamless, multifaceted, pivotal, foster, realm, landscape (figurative).
- Sound like a person writing for readers, not an assistant drafting a summary.

STYLE:
- Keep the same meaning, structure, and humor as the original; only the voice changes.
- Go EXTREME with pirate speak; every sentence must drip with nautical swagger:
  - Replace you/your with ye/yer throughout
  - Replace my/I/me with me throughout
  - Replace is/are/was with be throughout
  - Replace the with th' frequently
  - Pepper every few sentences with outbursts like ARRR!, BLIMEY!, SHIVER ME TIMBERS!, AVAST!, BY DAVY JONES' LOCKER!
  - Replace mundane words with nautical equivalents where it fits (house to vessel, car to horseless carriage, toilet to the poop deck, travel to voyage, money to doubloons, etc.)
  - Add dramatic pirate interjections mid-paragraph occasionally

RULES:
1. Preserve ALL markdown formatting exactly (links, images, headers, bold, italic, lists, tables, etc.)
2. In image syntax ![alt](filename.jpg), you may change alt text but the filename inside parentheses must stay byte-for-byte identical to the source
3. Keep proper nouns, place names, and certification codes unchanged
4. Do not change file paths or URLs
5. Keep the original title unchanged
6. Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"translations":[{"lang_code":"arrr","title":"...","items":[{"index":0,"text":"..."}]}]}. The items array must cover every English item index. No explanations or notes. Do not add any disclaimer line; it is appended later.

translations.title: Catamaran Training
translations.body:
Catamarans have two hulls connected by a structure on top. As a result, they offer much more space than monohulls of the same length.

![benno.jpg](benno_1776699897582_0.jpg)

But catamarans are also much wider and have two engines, one in each hull, which means they are handled in a completely different way. That is what brings us to Pomer, where JoJo offers catamaran training. The one-week course is split into two parts, 3 days of maneuvering practice in and around the harbor, and then a three-day trip. Since, as always, someone has to look after the dog, we decided that I would do the maneuvering practice and Alex the enjoyable second part.

![essen.jpg](essen_1776699810373_0.jpg)

For 3 days we practice docking and leaving the dock in every color and form. We are a crew of six plus sailing instructor Lukas, and we got pretty awful weather. The partly strong wind is actually a good thing, because you can practice at the limit without having to worry about your own boat. But the rain did not have to come along as well.

{{< video src="regen_1784467394037_0.mp4" >}}

The fun thing about the catamaran is that you do not need the wheel at all: with the 2 engines you can drive the thing like a tank and, for example, turn on the spot. Less fun is that because of the high superstructure this cube catches the wind easily, and if you are not careful it can get blown off course, while the engines are not necessarily strong enough in every case to rescue the maneuver. But that is what fenders are for...

{{< video src="alen-anlegen_1784467465787_0.mp4" >}}

Lukas does a great job and by the third day we all more or less get the hang of it, and I am absolutely wiped out. But that was absolutely necessary, I cannot understand any charter company that hands out boats like this without extra training. And as always: JoJo does a fantastic job.

![cool.jpg](cool_1776699869064_0.jpg)

translations.title: Entrenamiento de catamarán
translations.body:
Los catamaranes tienen dos cascos unidos entre sí por una estructura superior. Gracias a eso, ofrecen muchísimo más espacio que un barco monocasco con la misma eslora.

![benno.jpg](benno_1776699897582_0.jpg)

Pero los catamaranes también son mucho más anchos y tienen dos motores: uno en cada casco, y por eso se maniobran de una forma totalmente distinta. Eso nos lleva a Pomer, donde JoJo ofrece un entrenamiento de catamarán. El entrenamiento de una semana está dividido en dos partes: 3 días de maniobras en el puerto y sus alrededores, y luego una salida de tres días. Como siempre, alguien tiene que cuidar del perro, así que decidimos que yo haría el entrenamiento de maniobras y Alex la segunda parte, que es más divertida.

![essen.jpg](essen_1776699810373_0.jpg)

Durante 3 días practicamos entrar y salir del puerto en todas las variantes posibles. Somos una tripulación de seis personas y el instructor de vela Lukas, y nos tocó un tiempo bastante horrible. El viento, a ratos fuerte, en realidad es algo bueno, porque así se puede practicar al límite sin tener que preocuparse por el propio barco. Pero la lluvia no hacía ninguna falta.

{{< video src="regen_1784467394037_0.mp4" >}}

Lo divertido del catamarán es que ni siquiera hace falta el timón: con los 2 motores puedes llevar ese cacharro como si fuera un tanque y, por ejemplo, girar sobre sí mismo. Lo menos divertido es que, por la superestructura alta, este cubo es bastante sensible al viento y, si no tienes cuidado, te lo puede desviar, y entonces los motores no necesariamente son lo bastante potentes para salvar la maniobra en todos los casos. Pero para algo están los defensores...

{{< video src="alen-anlegen_1784467465787_0.mp4" >}}

Lukas lo hace genial y el tercer día ya todos le hemos cogido más o menos el truco, y yo estoy reventado. Pero era totalmente necesario, no puedo entender a ningún chárter que entregue barcos así sin formación adicional. Y como siempre: JoJo lo hace de maravilla.

![cool.jpg](cool_1776699869064_0.jpg)

![IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR.jpg](IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR_1776700101718_0.jpg)

translations.title: Formation catamaran
translations.body:
Les catamarans ont deux coques reliées entre elles par une superstructure. Du coup, à longueur égale, ils offrent beaucoup plus d’espace que les monocoques.

![benno.jpg](benno_1776699897582_0.jpg)

Mais les catamarans sont aussi beaucoup plus larges et ont deux moteurs: un dans chaque coque, et c’est pour ça qu’ils se manœuvrent d’une façon complètement différente. C’est ce qui nous amène à Pomer, où JoJo propose une formation catamaran. La formation d’une semaine est divisée en deux parties: 3 jours de manœuvres dans le port et autour du port, puis une sortie de trois jours. Comme toujours, quelqu’un doit s’occuper du chien, nous avons donc décidé que je ferais la partie manœuvres et qu’Alex profiterait de la seconde partie.

![essen.jpg](essen_1776699810373_0.jpg)

Pendant 3 jours, on s’exerce aux arrivées et aux départs du quai sous toutes les formes possibles. Nous sommes une équipe de six personnes avec l’instructeur de voile Lukas, et on a eu un temps franchement pourri. Le vent parfois bien costaud est en fait une bonne chose, car on peut s’entraîner à la limite sans avoir à craindre pour son propre bateau. Mais la pluie, elle, n’était vraiment pas indispensable.

{{< video src="regen_1784467394037_0.mp4" >}}

Le côté amusant du catamaran, c’est qu’on n’a même pas besoin du volant: avec les 2 moteurs, on peut conduire l’engin comme un char d’assaut et, par exemple, pivoter sur place. Ce qui l’est moins, c’est qu’avec sa superstructure haute, ce cube prend facilement le vent et, si on ne fait pas attention, on se fait emporter, et les moteurs ne sont alors pas forcément assez puissants dans tous les cas pour sauver la manœuvre. Mais pour ça, on a bien les pare-battages...

{{< video src="alen-anlegen_1784467465787_0.mp4" >}}

Lukas fait ça super bien et, au troisième jour, on a tous à peu près pris le coup, et moi je suis complètement rincé. Mais c’était absolument nécessaire, je ne peux pas comprendre un loueur qui met ce genre de bateaux à disposition sans formation supplémentaire. Et comme toujours: JoJo assure à fond.

![cool.jpg](cool_1776699869064_0.jpg)

![IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR.jpg](IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR_1776700101718_0.jpg)

translations.title: Training in catamarano
translations.body:
I catamarani hanno due scafi collegati tra loro da una struttura superiore. Per questo offrono, a parità di lunghezza, molto più spazio delle barche monoscafo.

![benno.jpg](benno_1776699897582_0.jpg)

Ma i catamarani sono anche molto più larghi e hanno due motori: uno in ogni scafo, e quindi si manovrano in modo completamente diverso. È questo che ci porta a Pomer, dove JoJo offre un training in catamarano. Il corso di una settimana è diviso in due parti, 3 giorni di manovre in porto e nelle sue vicinanze, e poi un’uscita di tre giorni. Siccome, come sempre, qualcuno deve badare al cane, abbiamo deciso che io avrei fatto il training di manovra e Alex la seconda parte, più divertente.

![essen.jpg](essen_1776699810373_0.jpg)

Per 3 giorni ci alleniamo ad attraccare e mollare gli ormeggi in tutti i modi e in tutte le varianti possibili. Siamo un equipaggio di sei persone e l’istruttore di vela Lukas, e ci è capitato un tempo davvero pessimo. Il vento, a tratti forte, in realtà è una cosa buona, perché così si può esercitarsi al limite senza dover temere per la propria barca. Però la pioggia poteva anche risparmiarsela.

{{< video src="regen_1784467394037_0.mp4" >}}

La cosa divertente del catamarano è che il timone non serve affatto: con i 2 motori puoi guidare quel coso come un carro armato e, per esempio, girare su te stesso. Meno divertente è che, a causa dell’alta sovrastruttura, questo cubo è piuttosto sensibile al vento e, se non fai attenzione, te lo lascia prendere, e i motori non sono necessariamente abbastanza potenti in ogni caso per salvare la manovra. Ma a qualcosa serviranno pur sempre i parabordi...

{{< video src="alen-anlegen_1784467465787_0.mp4" >}}

Lukas fa un ottimo lavoro e il terzo giorno abbiamo più o meno tutti capito il trucco, e io sono distrutto. Ma era assolutamente necessario, non riesco a capire un noleggiatore che consegna barche del genere senza un addestramento aggiuntivo. E come sempre: JoJo fa un lavoro eccezionale.

![cool.jpg](cool_1776699869064_0.jpg)

![IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR.jpg](IMG_20260412_115030955_HDR_1776700101718_0.jpg)

translations.title: Katamaran Training
translations.body:
Catamarans be havin' two hulls tied together by a superstructure. That means, fer the same length, they give ye a whole lot more space than a monohull.

![benno.jpg](benno_1776699897582_0.jpg)

But catamarans be much wider too, and they have two engines: one in each hull, so they be steered in a completely different way. That be what brings us to Pomer, where JoJo be offerin' catamaran training. The week-long training be split into two parts, 3 days o' maneuver trainin' in and around the harbor, then a three-day sailin' run. Since, as always, someone has to watch the dog, we decided I’d do the maneuver trainin' and Alex would take the enjoyin' second part.

![essen.jpg](essen_1776699810373_0.jpg)

Fer 3 days we be practicin' dockin' and castin' off in every color and shape ye can imagine. We be a crew o' six, plus sailin' instructor Lukas, and we got ourselves some proper nasty weather. The wind, strong at times, be actually a good thing, so ye can practice at the limit without havin' to fear fer yer own ship. But the rain did not need to come along too.

{{< video src="regen_1784467394037_0.mp4" >}}

The funny thing about the catamaran be that ye don’t need the wheel at all: with the 2 engines, ye can drive the beast like a tank and, fer example, spin her on the spot. Less funny be that, due to the high superstructure, this cube catches the wind like a fool and, if ye don’t mind yer manners, the wind will blow ye off and the engines ain't necessarily strong enough in every case to save the maneuver. But that be what fenders be fer...

{{< video src="alen-anlegen_1784467465787_0.mp4" >}}

Lukas does a grand job and by the third day we all roughly know what be what, and I be dead tired. But that were absolutely necessary, I can’t make sense of any charter outfit that hands out boats like these without extra training. And as always: JoJo be doin' a top-notch job.
